messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary

Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

Patient Name: [PATIENT NAME]
Medical Record Number: [MRN]

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 40-year-old female who was admitted with a complaint of lower extremity numbness and tingling. She subsequently developed left facial weakness, which had been previously diagnosed as Bell's Palsy. Neurological examination revealed bilateral decreased sensation to light touch, 4/5 strength in upper extremities, and 3/5 strength in lower extremities with no elicited reflex at any location. On day two of admission, she developed bilateral ptosis, urinary incontinence, and respiratory failure. On day three, the patient's ptosis worsened, and she also developed ophthalmoplegia. She was diagnosed with anti-GD1a antibody-positive Guillain-Barré Syndrome. The patient received five days of plasma exchange, IVIG, and high-dose solumedrol. Her condition began to improve on day seven and she was extubated on day eight. The vertical nystagmus was the first deficit to resolve, and the strength of her extremities recovered to 4+/5 in the upper extremities and 4-/5 in the lower extremities. She was transferred to an acute rehab unit after 20 days of hospitalization for continued management and rehabilitation.
Discharge Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Discharge Medications:
None

Discharge Instructions:
Follow up with primary care provider in 1-2 weeks
Return to work part-time as tolerated
Continue with physical therapy and rehabilitation program
Refrain from strenuous activity and prolonged sitting
Take care to prevent falls
If symptoms worsen, notify your healthcare provider immediately

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The admission is chiefly for Guillain-Barré syndrome (anti-GD1a positive), a demyelinating polyneuropathy, rather than its respiratory failure complication. GBS belongs to chapter G, diseases of the nervous system. Its three-character category is G61, inflammatory polyneuropathy (G61.0 Guillain-Barré syndrome).

CODE: G61
